items.title: Kenya Plans Automated Vehicle Checks as Road Deaths Climb
items.description: Transport CS Davis Chirchir unveiled automated vehicle checks and a Sh30 billion safety plan as NTSA targets 300,000 licences amid rising road fatalities.
content: Transport CS Davis Chirchir unveiled automated vehicle checks and a Sh30 billion safety plan as NTSA targets 300,000 licences amid rising road fatalities.

Roads and Transport Cabinet Secretary Davis Chirchir announced plans on November 26 to overhaul Kenyan motor vehicle inspections with automated testing centres, digital records, and expanded camera enforcement as road deaths rose nearly nine percent year-on-year.

Speaking at the Africa Road Safety Conference 2026 in Nairobi, Chirchir tied the reforms to Kenya's five-year Road Safety Action Plan for 2024 to 2028, valued at Sh30 billion. The government aims to cut fatalities by more than 30 percent over five years and halve road deaths and serious injuries by 2030.

The policy push coincided with an immediate festive-season crackdown by the National Transport and Safety Authority (NTSA). At Mlolongo in Machakos County on the same day, NTSA Director-General Nashon Odhiambo said the regulator plans to suspend at least 300,000 individual driving licences within a week over unpaid or uncontested instant fines.

Official figures presented by the Ministry of Roads and Transport show Kenya's road safety trajectory moving in the wrong direction. Annual fatalities increased from 4,748 in 2024 to 5,009 in 2025, a rise of 5.5 percent across 11,638 recorded crashes that also left 19,896 people with serious injuries.

By November 16, 2026, police and transport authorities had logged 4,613 road deaths, up from 4,238 during the same period in 2025. That represents 375 additional fatalities, or an 8.8 percent jump, ahead of December holiday travel when highway volumes typically surge.

Vulnerable road users, including pedestrians, motorcyclists, and passengers, accounted for 73 percent of crash victims in 2025, according to NTSA data. Chirchir estimated that road crashes drain approximately Sh450 billion from Kenya's economy each year, equivalent to between 5 percent and 8 percent of gross domestic product.

Under the ministry's Safe System framework, officials are pursuing a review of the Traffic Act, Cap. 403, alongside the Kenya Road Assessment Programme (KenRAP) to rank high-risk corridors and target accident blackspots during infrastructure planning. Over the past three months, the ministry also trained more than 4,000 public transport managers and drivers.

On the enforcement side, Chirchir said authorities are deploying speed cameras, automatic number plate recognition, and digital offence management with the National Police Service. NTSA surveillance already flagged 1.7 million vehicle and driver infractions over the preceding 30 days, with 740,000 speeding offences making up roughly 44 percent of all logged violations.

NTSA has already suspended 15,000 licences over the past month for speeding and reckless driving. Drivers affected by the new 300,000-licence suspension wave will have to pass a mandatory driving retest before returning to the road. Separately, the regulator plans to suspend inspection certificates for 25,000 commercial and public service vehicles caught speeding despite mandatory speed limiters, citing suspected device tampering.

Whether automated inspections will reach private motorists smoothly depends on resolving legal resistance that stalled earlier rules this year. In July and September 2026, the Senate formally annulled three statutory instruments gazetted by the ministry in February: the Traffic (Motor Vehicle Inspection) Rules, 2026, the Traffic (School Transport) Rules, 2026, and the NTSA (Operation of Commercial Vehicles) Regulations, 2026.

Those rules would have mandated annual inspections for private vehicles older than four years at fees between Sh1,000 and Sh2,000, alongside GPS telematics on school buses. Senators cited inadequate public participation and short compliance windows under the Statutory Instruments Act, while private school operators warned that scarce inspection bays in remote counties would penalise rural transport providers.

Funding remains the second decisive constraint. In his conference remarks, Chirchir acknowledged that achieving the five-year fatality reduction target depends on securing adequate financing and coordinated implementation across agencies. With the Senate blocking unconsulted rules and existing speed governors bypassed on thousands of vehicles, the ministry faces both a legislative test in redrafting Cap. 403 regulations and an operational test on highways.
The immediate test begins over the next seven days as NTSA executes its licence suspensions while Parliament awaits revised Traffic Act proposals from the ministry.

Gachagua bids for Somali vote with corruption accountability pledge
items.description: DCP leader Rigathi Gachagua has pledged accountability for North Eastern Kenya's public funds as he courts the Somali community vote ahead of the August 2027 election
content: The DCP leader promises North Eastern Kenya a reckoning with its political class — and a seat at the table of the sixth administration

Former Deputy President Rigathi Gachagua has made a direct pitch to the Somali community and North Eastern Kenya, promising that a future administration under his leadership would pursue accountability for public funds mismanaged in the region and end what he described as decades of political exploitation by local leaders.

In a statement directed at residents of Eastleigh, Kamukunji and the broader Somali community across the country, Gachagua was blunt about the scale of the grievance. “The Somali community in Kenya — a community of hardworking and astute businessmen and women — has been taken for granted by its leaders for far too long,” he said. “With over a trillion shillings disbursed to the North Eastern region since 2013, the only thing this community has received is incitement from busybodies in Nairobi, and looters of their resources building skyscrapers in Nairobi at the expense of residents in dire need of education, security, healthcare and other social amenities.”

The statement, which drew an enthusiastic response in Eastleigh, signals a deliberate and significant widening of Gachagua’s political coalition beyond the Mt Kenya base that remains his electoral heartland. Kamukunji MP Yusuf Hassan has already quit the Jubilee Party for Gachagua’s Democracy for the Citizens Party, a move analysts say could reshape political alignments in Nairobi ahead of 2027.

The arithmetic behind the outreach is straightforward. North Eastern Kenya lacks a dominant opposition political figure capable of rallying voters against the President — a gap the opposition, and Gachagua in particular, is actively seeking to exploit. The region’s Somali community, concentrated in Eastleigh and across Garissa, Wajir, Mandera and Isiolo counties, votes with notable cohesion when its leadership unites behind a candidate. For Gachagua’s sixth administration project, that cohesion could be transformative.

His pitch is built on a corruption accountability narrative that has been gaining unexpected traction in the north. Analysis of Gachagua’s political messaging suggests his corruption narrative is striking a chord in Northern Kenya, where voters are increasingly described as desperate to be freed from what observers characterise as the region’s entrenched political elite.

The government’s response has been equally pointed. Health Cabinet Secretary Aden Duale, speaking from Eastleigh, accused Gachagua of insulting the business community there, and rallied support for President William Ruto’s re-election, arguing that North Eastern Kenya and pastoralist counties would mobilise overwhelming support for the President. Duale specifically credited Ruto with resolving the community’s decades-long difficulties in accessing identity cards, passports and birth certificates — a genuine administrative grievance that has lingered since independence.

Opposition to Gachagua’s North Eastern push has taken pointed forms — a Mandera deputy governor compared supporting the DCP leader to eating pork, using a religious framing explicitly designed to discourage Muslim voters from backing him. Such interventions underscore the depth of establishment anxiety about what Gachagua’s coalition might become if the outreach succeeds.

Gachagua’s position on the Somali community has not always been uncomplicated. Earlier controversies around remarks about appointments and academic admissions prompted accusations that hardened some community leaders against him. He subsequently moved to distance himself from those characterisations, stating: “I have tremendous respect for that community; they are very honourable people. I do business with people from the Somali community, and their word is like a banker’s cheque.”

The current outreach appears designed to consolidate that reset and move decisively past earlier friction. By framing the issue as one of accountability — not identity — Gachagua is attempting to position himself as the candidate who will pursue corrupt local leaders rather than the community they represent. It is a distinction with real political potential in a region where frustration with its own political class runs genuinely deep.

Whether the Somali community and North Eastern Kenya ultimately move towards Gachagua in August 2027 will depend on factors beyond any single statement or visit. Local governors and MPs retain considerable influence over how their constituents vote, and most remain aligned with President Ruto. But the conversation has shifted. A year ago, a credible opposition pitch to North Eastern Kenya was barely visible. Today, it is one of the more consequential subplots of Kenya’s most closely watched election in a generation.

items.title: Sifuna takes his 2027 presidential pitch across America
items.description: Nairobi Senator Edwin Sifuna is touring six US states to build his Linda Mwananchi Movement's 2027 presidential campaign, opening a party office and courting diaspora voters
content: The Nairobi senator’s 17-day US diaspora tour opens a new front in Kenya’s most consequential pre-election season in a generation

Nairobi Senator Edwin Sifuna landed in the United States on 21 November 2026 to begin a 17-day diaspora engagement tour, taking his Linda Mwananchi Movement’s 2027 presidential campaign to Kenyan communities across six American states in a trip that doubles as a fundraising drive, a party-building exercise and a pointed message to the political establishment back home: the opposition is organised, it is coming, and it is not waiting to be invited.

The senator touched down at Newark Liberty International Airport in New Jersey in the early hours of that Saturday, where he was received by dozens of Kenyans waving flags and chanting slogans. The tour began with the official opening of a Linda Mwananchi Movement office in Hackettstown, New Jersey, at noon — a symbolic act that planted the movement’s first permanent institutional flag on American soil.

From New Jersey, the tour moved to Maryland and Washington DC between November 23 and 26, featuring a business community dinner, an East Africa politics and policy forum, engagements with local elected officials, a women’s brunch and a youth dialogue session. The itinerary then stretches to Texas, Washington State and California, concluding with a Silicon Valley dinner on 7 December.

The scale and structure of the tour are deliberate. This is not a goodwill visit. It is a campaign, and Sifuna knows it. A recent Trends Insight for Africa poll placed the Nairobi senator at 31 per cent alongside President William Ruto among preferred presidential candidates for 2027 — a number that would have been unthinkable twelve months ago for a politician whose national profile, while formidable in Nairobi, had not previously translated into presidential-scale numbers. The diaspora tour is designed to consolidate that momentum, build financial muscle, and demonstrate that the Linda Mwananchi Movement has the organisational seriousness to compete at the highest level.

The diaspora audience is not merely symbolic. Kenyans living in the United States send home hundreds of millions of dollars annually and represent a growing constituency of politically engaged citizens who have watched their country’s governance from a distance — often with a clarity that proximity occasionally blurs. For Sifuna, they are potential voters in a diaspora vote that Kenya continues to promise but has not yet delivered, potential donors to a movement still building its financial base, and an audience of respected voices whose endorsement carries weight back home.

In Maryland, Sifuna addressed Kenyan communities with the directness that has made him one of the opposition’s most watchable figures. He returned to a theme he has pursued in the Senate — the ballooning cost of Talanta Stadium, whose projected budget has risen from below KSh20 billion to approximately KSh45 billion, with an Auditor General’s finding of a KSh10 billion variance that has not been satisfactorily explained. At diaspora gatherings, he argued that the cost of a single stadium could have funded multiple comparable facilities across the country — money that, in his telling, represents precisely the kind of governance failure the 2027 election must correct.

The sharpest moment of the tour came when Sifuna recounted a private exchange with former Deputy President Rigathi Gachagua. Speaking to cheering crowds, he revealed what Gachagua had told him: “Sifuna, even if we supported you to become president, there are people you would have to imprison. Do you have a list of people you want to see jailed?” The crowd’s roar of approval captured everything about the moment: the frank acknowledgement of accountability as a political weapon, the implicit admission that those in power know what they did, and the dawning realisation among the opposition that the question of consequences is now firmly on the 2027 agenda.

In Maryland, Sifuna struck a note of opposition unity while also being candid about the electoral arithmetic. Speaking during his diaspora engagement, he said the opposition must put aside personal differences and embrace political cooperation, warning that going into the election as divided groups could weaken their chances. “I don’t want to obtain power by pretending to be something that I am not,” he told the crowd.

That message lands in a complicated landscape. The United Opposition grouping — which includes Gachagua’s Democracy for the Citizens Party, Wiper Party leader Kalonzo Musyoka and other formations — has yet to settle on a single presidential candidate, and the internal negotiations are likely to become Kenya’s most consequential political drama between now and the August 2027 election date. Sifuna’s position is delicate: he is both a potential candidate himself and an advocate for unity, two postures that will eventually require resolution.

The Kenya he is campaigning against is a country under acute economic pressure. The cost-of-living crisis that fuelled the Gen Z uprising of 2024 has not fully abated. Fuel prices remain stubbornly high. Youth unemployment continues to bite. The government’s tax agenda — which triggered historic street protests — cast a long shadow over its remaining term. For many Kenyans both at home and in the diaspora, 2027 is not an abstract political event. It is the most urgent practical question of their immediate lives.

Sifuna understands this. His pitch — framed around a “linda mwananchi” philosophy, meaning protect the citizen — deliberately positions him as the candidate of economic justice rather than tribal arithmetic. It is a frame that travels well in diaspora settings, where Kenyans often experience their national identity more than their county identity, and where the politics of the village can feel less urgent than the politics of the state.

Whether the momentum of a diaspora tour translates into electoral viability at home is a question Kenya’s political history answers cautiously. Diaspora enthusiasm has rarely determined the outcome of a Kenyan election. Ground organisation, ethnic bloc management, financial firepower and the machinery of incumbency have tended to matter more. Sifuna himself acknowledged as much, noting that Ruto retains formidable political muscle and that the opposition must be honest about the scale of the task ahead.

But what the tour has achieved, beyond the offices opened and the dinners held, is to establish Sifuna as a figure who takes the diaspora seriously at a time when the diaspora increasingly takes itself seriously. In an election cycle where every percentage point and every shilling of campaign funding will matter, that is not a small thing.

Kenya’s political road to August 2027 runs, in part, through the ballrooms and community halls of Maryland, New Jersey and California. Edwin Sifuna got there first — and in Kenyan politics, the candidate who shows up consistently tends to be the one the voters remember.

Transport CS Chirchir Announces Tougher Vehicle Inspection, Enforcement on Kenyan Roads
items.description: Kenya plans automated vehicle inspections and digital enforcement under a KSh 30bn action plan targeting a 30% fall in road deaths over five years in Kenya.
content: PAY ATTENTION: TUKO is in WhatsApp Channels now! Subscribe and read news in your favourite messenger.

Transport Cabinet Secretary Davis Chirchir has outlined plans to overhaul motor vehicle inspections in Kenya, introducing automated testing facilities and digital systems as part of a broader push to make roads safer across the country.
Chirchir made the announcement on Thursday, 26 November, at the Africa Road Safety Conference, which was convened by KCB Group and the Global Road Safety Partnership.

The CS said the government aimed to cut road fatalities by more than 30% over the next five years, with a longer-term goal of reducing deaths and injuries by at least 50% by 2030. He reaffirmed the Ministry of Roads and Transport's commitment to achieving those targets through a range of interventions.

He added that enforcement on the roads would be intensified, with authorities cracking down on speeding, drunk driving, dangerous overtaking, overloading and reckless driving. Technology will play a central role in that effort.
Chirchir also announced the establishment of the Kenya Road Assessment Programme (KenRAP), designed to identify high-risk sections of road and prioritise remedial work at accident blackspots.

On public transport, he said operator accountability was being strengthened alongside professional driver training. More than 4,000 public transport personnel and drivers completed training in the past three months, according to the CS.
All these measures fall under the KSh 30 billion Road Safety Action Plan covering 2024 to 2028, which also addresses motorcycle safety and improved enforcement capacity.
ENA Coach issues reminder notice to mums travelling with minors

The announcement arrives against a contentious backdrop. Earlier this year, the National Transport and Safety Authority (NTSA) had proposed rules requiring private vehicles older than four years to undergo annual inspections covering brakes, tyres, steering systems and other safety-critical components.

In July, however, the Senate annulled those rules, raising concerns that the implementation window was too short and that existing inspection facilities were insufficient to handle the volume of private vehicles. Senators also warned that the shortage of inspection centres could leave motorists vulnerable to harassment by enforcement officers.

Chirchir's latest statements suggest the government is pressing ahead with its road safety agenda despite that legislative setback, with a greater emphasis on automated infrastructure to address the capacity concerns that derailed the earlier proposals.

items.title: Kenya Airways Issues Early Warning as Fuel Costs Surge, Earnings Decline
items.description: Kenya Airways warns 2026 earnings could fall at least 25% as fuel costs reach half of operating expenses, following a KSh 17.2bn loss in 2025 amid fuel surge.
content: Search option is now available at TUKO! Feel free to search the content on topics/people you enjoy reading about in the top right corner ;)

Kenya Airways has issued a formal profit warning to investors, disclosing that its earnings for the financial year ending 31 December 2026 are expected to drop by at least 25% compared to 2025 figures.

The announcement, signed by Board Chairman Kiprono Kittony on 26 November 2026, cited soaring fuel costs linked to the ongoing Middle East conflict and widespread supply chain disruptions as the primary drivers of the anticipated decline.
The warning was issued in line with Kenya's Capital Markets (Securities) (Public Offers, Listing and Disclosures) Regulations, 2023.
The Board acknowledged that passenger demand across the aviation sector remains robust, but said external pressures have continued to weigh heavily on the airline's performance.
CS Wandayi pledges to protect Kenyans from unreasonable electricity costs
PAY ATTENTION: TUKO is in WhatsApp Channels now! Subscribe and read news in your favourite messenger.
Fuel costs at Kenya Airways jumped 72% in the first half of 2026, with acting CEO George Kamal stating that fuel now represents up to 50% of total operating costs.

The International Air Transport Association projects jet fuel will average USD 152 (approximately KSh 19,600) per barrel in 2026, nearly 70% above the 2025 average of USD 90 (approximately KSh 11,600).
African carriers face an additional burden, paying around 17% more than the global average owing to limited local refining capacity, transport costs, and taxation.
The Middle East conflict has also forced airlines to reroute flights around affected airspace, stretching journey times and burning more fuel on connections between Africa, Europe, and Asia.

Kenya Airways did attract additional passengers redirected away from Gulf transit hubs, with load factors reaching as high as 99% on select routes, but the sharp rise in operating costs offset much of that revenue gain.
Trump announces fresh tariffs on 14 countries after Supreme Court ruling

The 2026 warning builds on a troubled recent history. In 2025, the airline posted a net loss of KSh 17.2 billion, reversing a net profit of KSh 5.4 billion recorded in 2024, which had been the carrier's first annual profit in over a decade.
Total income fell to KSh 161.5 billion in 2025, down from KSh 188.5 billion the previous year.

Much of that decline stemmed from the temporary grounding of three Boeing 787-8 Dreamliner aircraft due to supply chain difficulties, which cut capacity by 18% and reduced passenger numbers by roughly 13%.

The first half of 2026 showed no meaningful recovery. Although revenue grew 9% to KSh 81 billion, the airline still posted a loss after tax of KSh 16.1 billion, compared to KSh 12.2 billion over the same period in 2025.

Finance costs climbed 11.1% to KSh 12.4 billion, the basic loss per share reached KSh 2.94, and negative equity widened to KSh 132.1 billion from KSh 118.3 billion, with total liabilities rising 6% to KSh 315.3 billion.

Looking ahead to 2027, the airline said it would prioritise restoring its full fleet, reducing costs, conserving cash, and completing a capital-raising exercise designed to stabilise its balance sheet and support long-term growth.

items.title: Absa Bank Kenya Reports Kshs. 15.3 Billion Profit After Tax for Nine Months to September 2026
items.description: Absa Bank Kenya PLC recorded a return on equity of 19.9%, reflecting continued business resilience and the execution of its customer-focused growth strategy
content: Absa Bank Kenya PLC has reported a profit after tax of Kshs. 15.3 billion for the nine months ended September 30, 2026, supported by growth in customer lending, deposits and total assets, alongside strong capital and liquidity positions.
Absa Bank Kenya PLC recorded a return on equity of 19.9%, reflecting continued business resilience and the execution of its customer-focused growth strategy amid a lower interest rate environment.
According to its nine-month financial performance, customer assets grew by 11% to Kshs. 342.5 billion, while customer deposits increased by 6% to Kshs. 408 billion.

Total assets rose by 9% to Kshs. 604.1 billion, crossing the Kshs. 600 billion milestone for the first time and strengthening the bank’s capacity to finance businesses, households and key sectors of the Kenyan economy.
The growth in customer financing reflects increased support for individuals, entrepreneurs and businesses seeking capital to invest, expand operations and achieve their financial ambitions.
Customer deposits also increased, highlighting continued confidence in Absa Bank Kenya as a financial partner and the growing relevance of its banking solutions.
The bank said its balance sheet expansion was driven by deeper customer relationships and increased access to financial services.
Absa Bank Kenya posts Sh10.5 billion half-year profit
Absa Bank Kenya generated total revenue of Kshs. 44.7 billion during the nine-month period, supported by balance sheet growth and disciplined management of funding costs.
Net interest income stood at Kshs. 32.3 billion, recording growth in each successive quarter, while non-interest income contributed Kshs. 12.4 billion.
The bank said its third quarter delivered its strongest revenue performance of 2026, reflecting sustained business momentum despite the lower interest rate environment.

Commenting on the results, Absa Bank Kenya Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer Yusuf Omari said the performance demonstrated customer confidence and the strength of relationships built across the bank’s franchise.

“Our nine-month performance reflects the trust that customers continue to place in Absa and the strength of the relationships we have built across our franchise. In a lower interest rate environment, we remained focused on supporting our customers’ ambitions through accessible financing, innovative solutions and seamless banking experiences,” said Omari.
He added that the customer-led approach supported growth in both lending and deposits, with momentum building throughout the year.
The bank continued to strengthen its portfolio quality while maintaining disciplined cost management and investing in technology, talent and business transformation.
Its cost-to-income ratio closed at 42%, remaining within the bank’s strategic plan.
Asset quality also improved, with the non-performing loans (NPL) ratio declining to 9.8%, which the bank said remained below industry levels.
The loan loss ratio improved to 2.0%, reflecting better portfolio performance and effective risk management.
Absa Bank Kenya’s capital adequacy ratio stood at 19.3%, while liquidity reserves were maintained at 44.7%, providing a strong financial position to support future lending and business growth.
The bank’s return on equity of 19.9% also demonstrated its continued ability to generate value for shareholders.
Absa commits Shs230M to new global multi-asset investment fund
Digital transformation remained a key pillar of Absa Bank Kenya’s growth strategy during the reporting period.
One of the notable developments was the launch of Absa Next , described by the bank as Kenya’s first integrated digital financial ecosystem.
The platform brings together banking, savings, investments, credit and lifestyle services in one digital environment accessible to both Absa customers and non-customers.
The initiative is designed to simplify access to financial services while providing customers with a more integrated experience beyond traditional banking.

Absa also expanded its affluent banking proposition through the introduction of Kenya’s first co-branded travel and lifestyle credit card, extending customer benefits into travel and lifestyle services.
Absa Asset Management Limited strengthened its investment offering through the launch of two new Global Multi-Asset Special Funds.
The funds are denominated in Kenya shillings and US dollars, providing investors with additional investment options and opportunities to diversify their portfolios.
The launches form part of the wider group’s strategy to deepen customer engagement, strengthen its investment management business and diversify revenue streams.
Co-op Bank Q3 net profit hits Sh27.4bn; interim dividend rises 50pc
Strategic partnerships continued to play an important role in expanding Absa’s financial and non-financial solutions.
The bank said its collaborations enabled it to provide tailored solutions that respond to the changing needs of customers while supporting business development and economic inclusion.
In Kenya, Absa facilitated financing for solar-powered cold storage solutions aimed at addressing gaps in the agricultural value chain and reducing post-harvest losses.
The initiative seeks to strengthen agricultural productivity by improving storage infrastructure and helping farmers and other value-chain players preserve their produce.

The bank also supported the third edition of a hackathon in Kenya through an established partnership, providing a platform for young women to develop technology-driven solutions to practical challenges.
These initiatives demonstrate the bank’s continued focus on using financial services and strategic partnerships to promote innovation, sustainability and inclusive economic growth.
Absa Bank Kenya said it would continue investing in digital platforms, strategic partnerships and customer relationships as it pursues its ambition of becoming the financial partner of choice.

The bank’s strategy is anchored on its purpose of Empowering Africa’s tomorrow, together… one story at a time , with a focus on delivering customer-led innovation and sustainable value for customers, communities and shareholders.

“As we execute the next phase of our strategy, our ambition remains clear on being the financial partner of choice by delivering customer-led innovation, market-leading solutions and sustainable growth across all our businesses,” said Omari.
He noted that the bank’s strong capital position, expanding digital ecosystem and diversified franchise provided a solid foundation for capturing emerging opportunities and creating long-term value.

Absa Bank Kenya’s nine-month results highlight the resilience of its banking operations, supported by balance sheet expansion, improving asset quality, digital innovation and continued investment in Kenya’s economic development.

European Union Opens Applications for KSh 69 Million Cleaning Services Contracts in Kenya
items.description: The EU Delegation to Kenya seeks firms for a KSh 69 million Nairobi cleaning contract. Learn tender requirements, application process and 21 December deadline.
content: PAY ATTENTION: TUKO is in WhatsApp Channels now! Subscribe and read news in your favourite messenger.

The European Union Delegation to Kenya has invited cleaning service firms to apply for a framework contract to service its Nairobi offices, with the total estimated value of the arrangement standing at KSh 69 million (€460,000) over a period of up to 48 months.

The tender, published on 20 November 2026 on the EU's Tenders Electronic Daily platform under procedure identifier EEAS/DELKENN/2026/RP/0097, was issued by the European External Action Service (EEAS).
The contract covers cleaning services at the EU Delegation's offices located at Dunhill Towers, 19th Floor, 115 Waiyaki Way, Westlands, Nairobi.

The procurement is structured as a framework service agreement awarded on the basis of the best price-quality ratio, classified under CPV 90910000 for cleaning services.
PAY ATTENTION: TUKO is in WhatsApp Channels now! Subscribe and read news in your favourite messenger.
No reopening of competition is envisaged once the contract is awarded.
The procedure is restricted, meaning it runs in two stages. In the first stage, interested firms submit a request to participate.
Only shortlisted candidates from that stage will receive an invitation to submit a full tender in the second stage.
Applications are open to any economic operator meeting the selection criteria set out in the procurement documents .
All submissions should be made electronically through the eSubmission system on the EU's Funding and Tenders Portal. Requests sent by email or letter were not accepted.

Each applicant is required to hold an EU Login account and to register in the Participant Register, through which organisations receive a nine-digit Participant Identification Code (PIC) used as their unique identifier across EU procurement processes.

Firms already registered are instructed to use their existing PICs rather than create new entries.
Interested firms can access full tender details and submit their requests to participate before the deadline on December 21, 2026 at 09:00 Africa/Nairobi time.
Any submission received after that point will be liable to be rejected, with the timestamp generated by eSubmission serving as proof of timely delivery.
Throughout the procedure, direct contact between applicants and the contracting authority is prohibited except in exceptional circumstances.

The EU Delegation also noted that the invitation to participate carried no binding commitment on its part, and the authority reserved the right to cancel the procedure at any point before contract signature without owing compensation to any candidate.
All costs related to preparing and submitting a request to participate are to be borne by the applying firms.

In other news, the Australian High Commission in Nairobi has opened applications for multiple Senior Visa Processing Officer positions within its Department of Home Affairs, with successful candidates earning a starting monthly salary of KSh 244,216.

The full-time roles, available on permanent and fixed-term contracts, involve assessing visa applications, verifying documents, applying immigration policies and handling correspondence, with officers expected to work 37.5 hours weekly at the commission's Rosslyn offices.

Applicants must demonstrate strong English communication, analytical and computer skills, while prior visa decision-making experience and relevant tertiary qualifications are desirable but not mandatory.

Applications comprising a two-page CV and a one-page Statement of Claims addressing three selection criteria must be submitted as a single PDF to nair.admin@dfat.gov.au by December 9, 2026, at 4:30 p.m. Nairobi time.

items.description: KeNHA warns motorists of a Mombasa Road closure between Nyayo Stadium and Museum Hill on 29 November for a 21km World AIDS Day half marathon and delays expected.
content: Search option is now available at TUKO! Feel free to search the content on topics/people you enjoy reading about in the top right corner ;)

The Kenya National Highways Authority (KeNHA) has warned motorists of an expected traffic disruption along a busy section of Mombasa Road (A8) on Sunday, 29 November 2026, to accommodate a half marathon marking World AIDS Day.

The notice, signed by Director General Eng. Luka Kimeli and dated 27 November 2026, states that the stretch between Nyayo National Stadium Roundabout and Museum Hill Interchange will be affected from 6.00 am to 10.30 am.
The road closure will allow a 21-kilometre half marathon to proceed as part of the World AIDS Day 2026 commemorations.

The event requires the use of a portion of the busy Nairobi highway, necessitating a temporary suspension of normal traffic flow along the affected section for approximately four and a half hours.
KeNHA has urged all motorists planning to use the route during that window to plan their travel accordingly and expect significant delays or diversions.
The authority advised road users to follow the traffic management plan that will be in place and to cooperate fully with police officers and traffic marshals deployed along the corridor.
KeNHA did not specify alternative routes in the notice but indicated that guidance would be provided on-site by the officers managing the closure.
Motorists with enquiries can contact KeNHA through its toll-free line on 0800-211-244, its customer care line at 0700 423 606, or via email at complaints@kenha.co.ke.
The authority can also be reached through its official social media handles and website.

In other news, KeNHA will close the Lower Kabete-Ndumbuini/Kapenguria Road-Uthiru Interchange from December 2, 2026, to January 31, 2027, to facilitate reconstruction of its ramps, loops and slip roads.

The closure will affect motorists using the Nairobi-Nakuru Highway corridor, with KeNHA Director General Eng. Luka Kimeli urging drivers to follow traffic signs and instructions from police officers and marshals.

Nairobi-bound motorists heading towards Ndumbuini can use alternative routes through Kabete Technical, Leadway Petrol Station or the 87/Muhuri Interchange, while drivers from Rironi and Nakuru can turn at Muhuri Interchange and use Muhuri-Ndumbuini Road.
Motorists travelling from Ndumbuini, Uthiru and Kawangware have also been directed to use Marigoini Cabro Road, Ndumbuini Road, Uthiru Underpass or Muhuri Interchange depending on their destinations.

items.title: Okoth Obado Case: Sharon’s Family to Appeal 25-Year Sentence, Wants Former Governor Freed
items.description: Sharon Otieno's family plans to appeal Okoth Obado's 25-year sentence for her murder, seeking his acquittal as his lawyers also prepare an appeal.
content: Search option is now available at TUKO! Feel free to search the content on topics/people you enjoy reading about in the top right corner ;)
Harry Ivan Mboto is a Current Affairs and Politics Editor at TUKO.co.ke, covering crime and court news. Mboto has five years of journalism experience and joined TUKO.co.ke in 2024
The family of slain university student Sharon Otieno plans to appeal the 25-year prison sentence handed to former Migori Governor Okoth Obado for her murder, seeking to have him acquitted.
The family's lawyer, Anthony Opondo, confirmed that they intend to challenge the sentence, which was delivered by the High Court in Milimani on Friday, November 27, 2026.
Obado's legal team has also announced plans to file a separate appeal against the decision, setting the stage for further legal proceedings in the high-profile murder case.

The family's decision comes after Justice Cecilia Githua sentenced Obado to 25 years in prison for the September 2018 murder of Sharon, a second-year Rongo University student who was seven months pregnant at the time of her death. A DNA test subsequently confirmed that Obado was the father of the unborn child.

The court also handed Obado's former personal assistant, Michael Juma Oyamo, a 25-year prison sentence, while former Migori County employee Caspal Ojwang Obiero was sentenced to 18 years for their roles in the killing.
The sentencing followed a judgment delivered on July 23, in which Justice Githua found all three men guilty of murder after considering evidence from 42 prosecution witnesses and 81 exhibits.
Okoth Obado sentenced to 25 years in prison over murder of Sharon Otieno
During sentencing, Justice Githua described Obado as the principal architect of the murder, saying he provided the motive, money and instructions that facilitated the killing.
She said Oyamo coordinated the murder while Obiero offered logistical support.

Before sentencing, Sharon's parents made an emotional appeal, asking the court to consider a non-custodial sentence for Obado. They said the former governor's family had approached them seeking reconciliation and that they had forgiven him.

Sharon's mother, Melinda Auma Rangili, told the court that her daughter's three children needed financial support and that allowing Obado to serve a non-custodial sentence would give him an opportunity to help provide for them.

She added that sentencing him to death or life imprisonment would feel like experiencing another death in her family. Sharon's father, Douglas Zakaria Otieno, also accepted reconciliation with Obado's family but expressed anger towards Oyamo and Obiero.
The court further declined to award compensation or restitution to Sharon's family, saying there was insufficient evidence to determine the losses they had presented.

items.title: Nairobi bursary scandal: 4,919 learners received funds up to nine times
items.description: Auditor General Nancy Gathungu has exposed KSh2.06 billion in Nairobi County bursary irregularities, with 4,919 learners receiving funds up to nine times in one year.
content: Auditor General Nancy Gathungu exposes KSh2.06 billion in bursary irregularities at City Hall — money meant for Kenya’s most vulnerable students

Auditor General Nancy Gathungu has exposed a systematic looting of Nairobi County’s bursary and scholarship programme, revealing that 4,919 learners irregularly received multiple allocations — some up to nine times in a single academic year — across a three-year period in which KSh2.06 billion was dispensed without proper financial need assessments, in one of the most damning indictments of devolved governance Kenya has seen in recent years.

The report, covering the financial years ending June 2021 through June 2024, lays bare the mechanics of a scheme designed, ostensibly, to give Kenya’s most disadvantaged students a path to education. What it delivered instead was a feeding trough: a system so poorly supervised that the same beneficiaries returned to the queue repeatedly, collecting funds that were meant to be distributed once per academic year to genuinely needy learners who, in many cases, never received a shilling.

The core finding is as simple as it is scandalous. Awards were made without any assessment of applicants’ financial needs or social vulnerability — the most elementary requirement of any credible bursary programme. Nairobi County is among seven counties flagged by the Auditor General for bursary irregularities, with KSh301.4 million in unaccounted funds cited separately in the same reporting cycle. But the broader KSh2.06 billion figure represents the full scope of the period under review — money that flowed through Nairobi’s ward bursary and executive scholarship systems while the oversight mechanisms that should have caught the abuse were either absent or deliberately ignored.

The methodology of the fraud, as reconstructed from the audit findings, is not especially sophisticated — and that is precisely what makes it so troubling. A student or a connected intermediary submits an application. No means test is conducted. No cross-referencing is done against previous awards. The allocation is processed and paid. The same student submits again the following term, or the following year. And again. And again. Up to nine times. The ward office responsible for verification either did not check or chose not to. The supervisory layer above it either did not ask or chose not to notice. By the time KSh2.06 billion had moved through the system across three financial years, the pattern was institutional — not incidental.

Gathungu has previously warned, in her performance audit of bursary programmes nationally, that “despite multiple education funding mechanisms, many eligible learners continue to be left out as a result of delays, inconsistencies, and weak accountability in the allocation process.” The Nairobi findings confirm that those warnings were not abstract cautions. They were an accurate description of a system operating as a patronage mechanism rather than a welfare programme — one in which access to funds depended not on demonstrable need but on familiarity with the right people in the right offices.

The Auditor General’s report on Nairobi County flagged an estimated KSh20 billion in irregular and disputed spending at City Hall across multiple programmes — an astonishing aggregate for a county whose residents include some of the most economically marginalised urban populations in East Africa. The bursary scandal sits within that broader landscape of institutional failure, but it carries a particular moral charge. The Auditor General’s report for the financial year ending June 2024 detailed how Nairobi City County is rocked with massive irregularities and irregular expenditure amounting to billions of shillings spanning programmes from school feeding to housing to scholarships. The pattern is consistent across all of them: weak internal controls, missing documentation, and a beneficiary selection process that appears to have rewarded proximity to power over demonstrated need.

According to the Auditor General, without proper evidence of beneficiaries, the money may have ended in the pockets of officials managing the funds — a conclusion that transforms what might otherwise be characterised as administrative sloppiness into something far more deliberate. Sloppiness does not pay the same person nine times. Sloppiness does not systematically fail to conduct a needs assessment across 4,919 cases over three consecutive financial years. What the audit describes is a structured extraction of public resources from a programme designed to serve the poor, executed with sufficient consistency to suggest it was understood and accommodated at multiple levels of the county bureaucracy.

What makes the bursary scandal particularly corrosive is precisely the nature of the funds involved. This was not procurement fraud on a government infrastructure contract, where the harm, though real, is diffuse and abstract. This was money designated specifically for children — for school fees, books, uniforms, and the basic costs of remaining in education. Every multiple payment collected by a connected beneficiary or a fraudulent intermediary represents a student who sat at home, fell behind, dropped out, or borrowed against a family’s already strained resources because the county’s allocation for genuine need had already been captured by someone gaming the system. The human cost of that arithmetic — played out across thousands of households in Mathare, Kibera, Mukuru and Eastleigh — is immeasurable in audit terms but entirely real in consequence.

The political context surrounding the findings could not be more charged. With Kenya’s August 2027 General Election now fewer than nine months away, accountability — or its conspicuous absence — has become the defining fault line of competitive politics across the country. Opposition figures have made the misappropriation of devolved funds the centrepiece of their campaign narrative, arguing that billions allocated to counties since 2013 have enriched political elites rather than transformed the lives of ordinary Kenyans. Reports like this one hand that argument its most compelling evidence.

Gathungu’s audit sampled constituencies across six counties and found, among other systemic problems, stale and unpresented bursary cheques across multiple constituencies — funds allocated but never actually delivered to the students they were intended to reach. In Nairobi’s case, the problem runs in the opposite direction: money that was delivered — repeatedly — to those who had already received their entitlement, while the genuinely needy queued unserved. Both failures are products of the same underlying dysfunction: a bursary system built without the basic accountability infrastructure needed to ensure public money reaches the right people.

The remedies, in principle, are not complicated. Automation of the bursary application and disbursement process, cross-referencing of national identification details against award histories, mandatory means-testing before any allocation is processed, and real-time digital tracking of payments would, together, make the kind of multiple-payment fraud documented in Nairobi technically impossible to sustain. Gathungu’s national report noted that South Mugirango, Uriri, Mwala, Gatanga and Emgwen constituencies had fully automated their bursary processes, resulting in improved efficiency and transparency — proof that the solution exists and is affordable. What is missing is not technology. It is the political will to implement it in systems where the opacity of manual processes serves the interests of those who benefit from the current arrangement.

Gathungu’s reports do not name individual perpetrators. That is the job of the Ethics and Anti-Corruption Commission, the Director of Public Prosecutions, and the county assembly oversight committees to whom the reports are submitted. Whether those institutions choose to act on findings of this magnitude — or whether the reports join Kenya’s long archive of audit literature that is read, noted and quietly shelved — is the accountability question that matters most in the months ahead.

For the 4,919 learners identified as having received multiple irregular allocations, whatever consequences arrive will follow the slow arc of Kenyan judicial process. For the thousands of genuinely needy students across Nairobi’s most deprived wards who should have received that KSh2.06 billion and did not, the consequences are already written — in interrupted schooling, abandoned ambitions, and futures narrowed before they ever had the chance to open.

A bursary programme exists for one reason: to ensure that poverty is not destiny. In Nairobi County, between 2021 and 2024, it served a different purpose entirely — and the children who paid the price for that betrayal had no voice in any of it.

Africa Uncensored's investigative documentary, 'Beg, Borrow, Steal: Kenya's Budgeted Corruption and The China Connection', produced by veteran journalist John-Allan Namu, has been taken down following a court order obtained by individuals and entities named in the film.

Namu confirmed the development on Thursday, November 26, explaining that parties adversely mentioned in the exposé had secured an order from the court restraining publication of the documentary. He noted that although the order was not formally served on his team, they independently verified its authenticity before deciding to comply.

The film investigated allegations that more than KSh 30 billion intended for major Kenyan infrastructure projects was diverted through shell companies, questionable financial transactions, irregular tax arrangements and dubious contractors.
Its central inquiry was whether Kenya received full value for the billions borrowed to build roads and other infrastructure, or whether portions of those funds were siphoned into private networks.

The investigation drew on whistleblower accounts, banking records and tax investigations. It scrutinised two Chinese companies and their financial relationships with Kenyan businesses, raising questions about whether the government received the services and materials for which payments were made.

Among the key projects examined was the Nairobi Western Bypass, financed through a loan of approximately KSh 23.4 billion (USD 181 million) from China. The documentary questioned the value Kenyans received relative to what was borrowed and spent on the project.

The Kipevu Oil Terminal in Mombasa was also under the spotlight, with the film highlighting a figure of approximately KSh 21.5 billion in its examination of alleged financial irregularities connected to the project.

Last month, Namu called out a section of Kenyan podcasters for accepting large sums of money from politicians and passing it off as journalism.

The Africa Uncensored founder urged journalists to guard the profession and stamp out the culture of brown envelope.

items.title: EACC Chair Oginde Proposes Major Changes to Kenya’s Corruption Laws
items.description: EACC chairman David Oginde wants Kenya to review its legal framework on presumption of innocence, citing Tanzania's approach to criminal convictions in the fight against corruption.
content: Ethics and Anti-Corruption Commission (EACC) chairperson Bishop David Oginde has called for sweeping reforms to Kenya’s legal framework, arguing that suspects exploit the presumption of innocence to stall anti-corruption efforts.

Speaking at a breakfast meeting during the Annual Editors Convention in Mombasa County, Oginde suggested Kenya draw lessons from neighboring Tanzania to close legal loopholes and strengthen public accountability. The Kenya Editors Guild organized this year’s convention under the theme, “Navigating the Storm: Media Resilience on the Road to 2027.”

Oginde highlighted a recent Tanzanian law under which anyone convicted of an offense carries the burden of proving their innocence during an appeal, rather than retaining the presumption of innocence.
“Once a person has been convicted in Tanzania for any offense, they stand guilty until they prove themselves innocent,” Oginde said.
He contrasted that system with Kenya’s legal framework, where accused individuals retain the presumption of innocence until they exhaust the entire judicial process, including all appeals.

To illustrate how this plays out locally, Oginde pointed to the legal battles surrounding former Nairobi Governor Mike Sonko, noting that authorities only stopped him from running for office after his final appeal failed.
“This is the case that happened with Sonko [former Nairobi governor] when he was barred from contesting. Sonko was barred because he had exhausted all appeals mechanisms,” Oginde said.
According to the EACC chair, corruption suspects routinely use prolonged appeal processes to delay justice and cling to public positions, damaging national integrity.
“For us, you remain innocent until you have exhausted the whole judicial process. And people have exploited that provision to the detriment of our integrity in the country,” he said.

Oginde urged Kenyans to examine regional legal models and debate targeted constitutional and statutory amendments that could give anti-graft agencies sharper teeth. He noted that public awareness remains essential to building support for these legal changes.
“These are some things that we need to highlight and educate Kenya so that we can make relevant amendments to our laws so that we can deal with corruption,” he said.

items.title: Kipchoge Tells Kenya to "Dream Big" and Chase Africa's Second Marathon Major
items.description: Eliud Kipchoge, Kenya's two-time Olympic marathon champion, has called on the country to "dream big" and pursue Africa's second Marathon Major, The Star reported. The Nairobi-based daily said the distance-running grea…
content: Eliud Kipchoge, Kenya's two-time Olympic marathon champion, has called on the country to "dream big" and pursue Africa's second Marathon Major, The Star reported. The Nairobi-based daily said the distance-running great wants the World Marathon Majors, the sport's premier series of city marathons, to stage a race on Kenyan soil.

Kipchoge is the most decorated marathon runner Kenya has produced. Born in Kapsabet in Nandi County and long based at a training camp in Kaptagat in the Rift Valley, he became the first person to cover the marathon distance in under two hours when he ran 1:59:40 at the INEOS 1:59 Challenge in Vienna in 2019, a run staged behind rotating teams of pacemakers that was not eligible for official record purposes. His official world record of 2:01:09, set at the Berlin Marathon in 2022, stood until fellow Kenyan Kelvin Kiptum clocked 2:00:35 at the Chicago Marathon in 2023.

The World Marathon Majors sits at the summit of the city marathon circuit. The series launched in 2006 with five founding races in Boston, London, Berlin, Chicago and New York, and grew to six when Tokyo joined in 2013. The Sydney Marathon became the series' seventh race in 2025, while South Africa's Sanlam Cape Town Marathon has been lined up as Africa's first entry in the fold. A second African slot is now the open question, and it is that prize The Star reported Kipchoge wants Kenya to claim.

The majors are the biggest races in the sport. The New York City Marathon, the largest marathon in the world, regularly records more than 50,000 finishers, while Boston, the oldest annual marathon, first staged in 1897, holds a field of about 30,000 runners who must post qualifying times to enter. Berlin's flat, fast course has been the setting for most of the men's world records of the past two decades. Champions at the majors race for the richest prizes in road running, and the series also crowns a season-long points champion, a title Kenyan runners have taken repeatedly.

Kipchoge's own record in the series stands apart. He has won nine major titles: the Chicago Marathon in 2014, the London Marathon in 2015, 2016, 2018 and 2019, and the Berlin Marathon in 2015, 2017, 2018 and 2022. He also claimed two Olympic titles, winning the marathon in Rio de Janeiro in 2016 in 2:08:44 and defending it at the Tokyo Games in Sapporo in 2021 in 2:08:38. Only two other men in Olympic history, Ethiopia's Abebe Bikila and East Germany's Waldemar Cierpinski, have won back-to-back marathon gold medals.
Also read Marathon Debutant Ngetich Joins Defending Champion Jepkosgei in Valencia World Record Chase

Kipchoge built his career on the track, winning the 5,000 metres world title in Paris in 2003 at the age of 18, beating Morocco's Hicham El Guerrouj and Ethiopia's Kenenisa Bekele, before taking Olympic bronze in Athens in 2004 and silver in Beijing in 2008. The tradition behind him runs deep. Kenyan men have won three of the last five Olympic marathons, with Sammy Wanjiru taking Beijing in 2008 in 2:06:32 and Kipchoge winning in Rio and Tokyo, while Peres Jepchirchir took the women's Olympic marathon title in Tokyo. Catherine Ndereba, a four-time Boston Marathon winner, led the country's women before them.

Kenya already holds a central place on the global marathon map. The high-altitude training towns of Iten in Elgeyo Marakwet County and Kaptagat draw professional runners from around the world, and the capital stages the annual Nairobi City Marathon on its streets. Kenyan runners have also supplied a steady stream of winners at the biggest city races from London to Boston to New York. No Kenyan race, however, currently sits in the majors series.

Only three men in history have broken 2:02 over the official marathon distance: Kipchoge, Kiptum and Ethiopia's Kenenisa Bekele. Two of the three are Kenyan, and the men's world record has been held by a Kenyan since Kipchoge broke it in Berlin in 2018, passing from his 2:01:39 that day through his 2:01:09 in 2022 to Kiptum's 2:00:35 in Chicago.

By May 2023, she had relocated to Boston, Massachusetts with the three children, citing the need to protect them, particularly her teenage daughter Shirleen, from a toxic environment. She later said bluntly:

Kenya Needs Its Own AI Models, Data Centres And Energy, Ndemo Says
items.description: The former ambassador argues that locally trained models, built around African languages and contexts, are essential to protecting data, expanding access and creating jobs.
content: Kenya must build its own artificial intelligence infrastructure and train models in local languages if it is to retain control of its data, develop relevant AI applications and capture more economic value from the technology, Dr Bitange Ndemo has said.

Speaking during a session on Sovereign AI at the CIO100 Symposium & Awards 2026 in Diani, the former Ambassador to Belgium and the European Union argued that relying on foreign AI models exposes African countries to external decisions over access, data and the technologies their economies increasingly depend on.
“Everybody can actually make their own AI which understands the local context,” Ndemo said, arguing that models must be trained to understand local laws, cultures and languages.

He described AI as a child’s brain that needs to be trained and shaped by its environment. A model developed elsewhere, he argued, may not adequately understand the differences between Kenyan, Tanzanian and Ugandan law, or the social and cultural contexts in which people use technology.

For Ndemo, sovereignty goes beyond hosting data locally. It requires countries to develop the supporting infrastructure, including data centres, reliable energy, connectivity, skilled engineers and locally trained language models.
Local languages are central to AI adoption
Ndemo said the limitations of foreign models become particularly significant when AI is expected to address problems rooted in local economic and social realities.

He argued that African languages do not always have direct equivalents for concepts such as data, productivity and predictability. Without the vocabulary to communicate these ideas accurately, he said, AI systems risk reproducing gaps in how development challenges are understood and addressed.
He used poverty as an example, arguing that efforts to address it have often failed to communicate the practical knowledge people need to improve their livelihoods.

In agriculture, he said, farmers need information that helps them use fewer resources to produce more. Locally trained models could help communicate such knowledge in languages and contexts that communities understand.

Ndemo also pointed to education, arguing that learning in a familiar language can improve comprehension. Personalised AI, he said, could adapt how information is delivered to an individual’s pace of understanding, potentially reaching learners who struggle in conventional classroom settings.

He said locally developed models could also help bridge the gap between formal education and practical knowledge, using the example of rural builders who understand roof angles through experience even when they may not connect that knowledge to classroom mathematics.
Sovereignty requires infrastructure and energy
Ndemo warned that dependence on foreign AI providers creates strategic risks for countries that lack control over the models they use.

He raised the possibility of an external provider restricting access to its services following a political or commercial decision, leaving businesses and public institutions without systems on which they have come to rely.
He also questioned the value African countries receive when they provide data that can be used elsewhere to develop commercial products, including medicines.
His argument was that African countries should retain greater control over the data and infrastructure needed to develop their own AI capabilities.

Energy, he said, is a critical part of that ambition. He urged African governments and investors to direct more capital towards electricity generation, arguing that data centres and GPU infrastructure require reliable and affordable power.

Citing Ethiopia’s investments in electricity generation, Ndemo said the country had moved ahead with large-scale energy projects that could support industrial activity and emerging technology industries.
He argued that Kenya should use available land and energy resources to attract infrastructure investment, create employment and support a growing cloud economy.
Building a talent pipeline and local AI industry
Ndemo said sovereign AI would also require sustained investment in engineers and other technical professionals who can build, train and maintain local systems.

He argued that developing local language models could create opportunities for African startups, content creators and technology businesses, while allowing countries to address challenges that imported systems may not adequately understand.

Among the potential applications he cited was healthcare. He described the use of smartphone-based tools to help health workers identify possible tuberculosis cases, illustrating how AI could support earlier diagnosis and intervention.
He also said locally developed systems could help create jobs by enabling businesses to build products and services around models trained for African markets.
Ndemo disclosed that he was working towards developing a Kenyan AI model and was seeking local partners willing to test and support the initiative before wider commercial participation.

He said the intention was to make a basic model available for people to begin using, with a broader national AI service offering that could support developers and businesses. He invited interested organisations to engage with the initiative, including through potential subscriptions to solutions built on the model.

His message to technology leaders was that AI sovereignty should not be reduced to a debate about foreign versus local software. It should be treated as a national capability involving energy, infrastructure, data, skills and language.
“Everything needed already exists. Only the model is missing,” Ndemo said.

Kenya unveils new renewable energy projects as global delegates convene in Naivasha
items.description: More than 1,000 delegates from 80 countries have converged at Olkaria in Naivasha for the 3rd Annual Sustainable Energy Conference to discuss progress in green energy development and explore opportunities to address existing gaps in the sector.
content: More than 1,000 delegates from 80 countries have converged at Olkaria in Naivasha for the 3rd Annual Sustainable Energy Conference to discuss progress in green energy development and explore opportunities to address existing gaps in the sector.

The three-day conference, themed Powering Africa in the Green Industrial Revolution, has brought together stakeholders from the energy, finance, government and private sectors to explore investment opportunities and partnerships aimed at accelerating the transition to sustainable energy.

Speaking during the conference, KenGen CEO Engineer Peter Jenga said the company has identified several potential renewable energy projects currently undergoing feasibility studies, which are expected to inject additional megawatts into the national grid.
Jenga said the projects include a 42.5-megawatt solar power plant, an 8.6-megawatt Gogo hydroelectric power project and an 80.3-megawatt geothermal power plant.

“We have already completed the assessment of EPC contractors for a 42.5-megawatt solar power plant. We are also completing the assessment for the Gogo hydro power plant, which will generate 8.6 megawatts,” said Jenga.
He added that the company is exploring small hydro-power opportunities across the country to address challenges associated with reliance on conventional hydro-power generation.
One of the identified sites is in Webuye, where preliminary assessments indicate the potential to generate 26 megawatts of electricity.

The company is also considering wind energy development in Marsabit, which Jenga says has the potential to generate approximately 1,000 megawatts, with an initial 200-megawatt project being considered.
Meanwhile, Canada has reaffirmed its commitment to supporting Kenya’s energy transition through investment, technical cooperation and technology transfer.
Canadian High Commission Head of Cooperation Sophie Grace said Canada is keen to explore opportunities in Kenya’s energy sector, including nuclear energy and drilling technologies.
She noted that Canada’s extensive experience in energy production could help Kenya strengthen its capacity and position itself as a regional energy exporter.
“We would really like to help support Kenya to move into becoming a large exporter in the region, and that is one of our goals in this collaboration,” said Grace.

Energy and Petroleum Regulatory Authority (EPRA) Director of Economic Regulation and Strategy Dr John Mutua called for stronger public-private partnerships to mobilise investments and accelerate the implementation of viable energy projects.
Mutua said collaboration with private investors remains critical in achieving Kenya’s energy transition while ensuring consumer protection and sustainability in the sector.

“As we work towards energy transition and ensuring that Kenya is powered with renewable energy, we hope to match the needs of investors while protecting consumers and ensuring a sustainable energy sector,” he said.

The discussions come as Kenya pursues its ambition of transitioning to a predominantly renewable energy-powered economy by 2034, with strategic partnerships, increased investment and technology transfer expected to play a central role in achieving the target.

The three-day conference is expected to provide a platform for stakeholders to strengthen international cooperation, identify investment opportunities and develop strategies to accelerate Africa’s green industrial revolution.

Kenya drops its FlexPay case, the third fintech reversal since 2022
items.description: FlexPay, the trading name of Flexitech Group Limited, ran a save-now, buy-later service with Naivas Supermarkets under a seven-year agreement signed in February 2021 and due to run until 2028. Shoppers paid in instalments at Naivas tills, FlexPay kept a 5% commission, and the rest was supposed to reach Naivas within 24 hours. The arrangement
content: FlexPay, the trading name of Flexitech Group Limited, ran a save-now, buy-later service with Naivas Supermarkets under a seven-year agreement signed in February 2021 and due to run until 2028. Shoppers paid in instalments at Naivas tills, FlexPay kept a 5% commission, and the rest was supposed to reach Naivas within 24 hours.

The arrangement worked for about five years before Naivas said FlexPay stopped remitting collections in early 2026, leaving a shortfall of Sh31.2 million, roughly $240,000. The Directorate of Public Prosecutions recommended theft by agent charges in August.

Detectives arreste d two of the four executives eventually named, Martin Kariuki Maina and Johnson Gituma Mwangi, on 1 September. The other two, chief growth officer Dennis Karanu Mwangi and director Richard Machomba, also faced possible prosecution.
The High Court declined in early October to halt the prosecution , ruling that reputational harm alone does not justify stopping a criminal case already filed.

The case turned anyway. In a letter dated 6 November, the Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions reversed its own decision , telling the Nairobi Regional Criminal Investigation Officer that a further review of the Directorate of Criminal Investigations’ evidence found the dispute civil in nature.

It directed that the file be closed with no further police action and that Naivas be advised to seek civil redress instead. The partnership that had processed more than Sh3 billion in customer payments over five years was already over by the time that letter went out.

Four days later, High Court judge Roseline Aburili barred police and prosecutors from arresting, detaining or charging the four executives while a separate constitutional petition they had filed, accusing Naivas of using police to recover a commercial debt, is heard.

Public interest is not merely served by securing convictions at all costs, it is primarily anchored on the integrity of the administration of justice. The public must have confidence that the criminal process is even handed.
FlexPay disputed being an agent of Naivas at all, telling the court it was a corporate customer operating a credit account, buying goods on credit and settling the balance periodically.

It counterclaimed that Naivas owed it Sh24 million in unreimbursed customer loyalty points and more than Sh300 million in losses it blamed on price manipulation by Naivas staff, plus a further Sh3.07 million it says it paid Naivas during the dispute but was never credited.
Neither the prosecutors’ decision nor the High Court ruling settled which side’s financial claims are correct. Both remain open questions for whatever court eventually hears the underlying debt.

Kenya’s Asset Recovery Agency filed a money laundering and card fraud suit against the Nigerian fintech Kora and a second firm, Kandon Technologies, in July 2022. The court froze both companies’ accounts for six months while the agency investigated.

By November, the Directorate of Criminal Investigations told the court the allegations were not established and asked that its communication be treated as final. Kora’s chief operating officer said the company had always maintained its innocence.

The Asset Recovery Agency also filed a money laundering case against Flutterwave in 2022, alleging that funds in its Kenyan accounts were proceeds of crime. An initial Sh52.5 million portion of that case was closed in March 2023.

A second, linked case involving $3 million held with co-accused firms Adguru and Hupesi Solutions dragged on until November 2023, when the agency withdrew it after what it called further investigation.

The judge who allowed the withdrawal did not simply grant it. He criticised the agency for filing serious proceedings before finishing its own investigation, calling the conduct inappropriate, negligent, reckless and absurd for an investigative body, and ordered that any resulting liability fall personally on the agency’s director and investigating officer rather than on public funds.
It was inappropriate, negligent, reckless and absurd to an investigative agency.

FlexPay’s case began with a private business partner, Naivas, taking a contractual payment dispute to the police. Kora’s and Flutterwave’s cases began with the state’s own Asset Recovery Agency acting on its own suspicion of money laundering, with no named commercial counterparty driving the complaint.

What connects all three is the outcome. A Kenyan authority with the power to freeze accounts and arrest executives moved first and investigated the underlying claim afterwards, and in each case the claim did not hold up once examined.

Neither the prosecutors nor the High Court has ruled on whether Naivas or FlexPay is actually owed money, so the Sh31.2 million claim, FlexPay’s Sh24 million loyalty point counterclaim and its Sh300 million price manipulation allegation all remain unresolved.

Naivas has not said publicly whether it intends to pursue civil proceedings, as prosecutors advised. It is also not yet clear whether the four executives’ constitutional petition will still proceed now that the underlying investigation file has already been closed.
The first thing to watch is whether Naivas actually files a civil claim, since prosecutors advising that route does not guarantee it happens.

The second is whether three reversed cases in four years change how Kenya’s Asset Recovery Agency and the Directorate of Criminal Investigations screen a complaint against a fintech before freezing accounts or making an arrest, since each case so far has cost the accused company months of frozen funds and public suspicion before the state concluded it had moved too soon.

Kenya woos foreign investors to partner with Kenya on development projects
items.description: Mudavadi urged foreign investors to bring capital, technology and expertise at Equity Group's investment roadshow today.
content: Kenya is courting international investors to bring capital, technology and expertise to fund development, as the government leans on private businesses to complement stretched public resources.

The push was the main theme of Equity Group’s five-day Trade and Investment Roadshow. The event opened in Nairobi on November 25 and has brought together more than 650 investors, business leaders, policymakers and development partners from 54 countries.
Prime Cabinet Secretary and Foreign and Diaspora Affairs Cabinet Secretary Musalia Mudavadi said Kenya wants investors who bring more than money.
“Kenya welcomes you, bringing not only capital, but also technology, expertise, market knowledge and confidence in the possibilities of our people,” said Mr Mudavadi.

“Join us as partners in building competitive and sustainable projects that generate attractive returns while creating jobs, expanding opportunities and delivering lasting benefits for our economy and society.”
Equity Group Chief Executive James Mwangi said the private sector’s role in financing development has long been underestimated.

“Businesses are creating thousands of jobs, generating wealth and contributing billions in taxes. The private sector is well positioned to work alongside governments in financing development, driving economic growth and creating opportunities for our people,” said Dr Mwangi.

Kenya Private Sector Alliance (KEPSA) Chief Executive Carole Kariuki said local businesses bring established supply chains, entrepreneurial expertise and manufacturing capability to partnerships with foreign investors.

She said such partnerships could help Kenyan firms reach wider markets. She also called for a predictable policy environment to attract investment in sectors such as e-mobility, agro-processing and digital services.
Mary Peschka, the International Finance Corporation’s regional director for Eastern Africa, said investors need mechanisms that reduce risk before they commit capital for the long term.
“Through risk-sharing solutions, sound financial structures and local-currency financing, we can help give investors the confidence to commit capital for the long term,” said Ms Peschka.
She identified regulatory reforms, a pipeline of bankable projects and stronger regional supply chains as key to drawing investment.

The roadshow, which ends on November 29, is connecting investors with government officials and Kenyan companies to identify partnerships in manufacturing, agriculture, financial services and other productive sectors.
The initiative is part of Equity Group’s Africa Recovery and Resilience Plan, which aims to link African businesses with capital, technology, markets and expertise.
